profile.feeling: White – walls, snow, milk, white wine.

examples.tr: I’m having a glass of white wine.

etymology.text: From Middle High German wīȥ, from Old High German wīȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *hwīt, from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweytos (“bright; shine”).

funFacts: From the Indo-European root for “bright, shine” – the same root as Russian свет (light).
English white and German weiß are one Germanic word.
pitfalls: weiß is also a form of wissen: ich weiß / er weiß = I know / he knows. Die Wand ist weiß – Ich weiß es.
subtleties: As a noun a colour is neuter and capitalised: das Weiß (ein helles Weiß).
Comparison exists but is rare for colours: weißer, am weißesten.

profile.feeling: Black – black coffee, a black phone; and “illegal” in schwarzfahren.

examples.tr: He always rides without a ticket.

etymology.text: From Middle High German swarz, from Old High German swarz, from Proto-West Germanic *swart, from Proto-Germanic *swartaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swerd- (“dirty, dark, black”). Compare Dutch zwart, English swart and swarthy, Yiddish שוואַרץ (shvarts).

funFacts: English swarthy (dark-skinned) is a cousin of schwarz.
pitfalls: schwarz- in verbs means “illegal”: schwarzfahren (ride without a ticket), schwarzarbeiten (work off the books).
subtleties: As a noun a colour is neuter and capitalised: das Schwarz (ein helles Schwarz).
Comparison with umlaut: schwärzer, am schwärzesten (schwarzer also exists).

profile.feeling: Red – red wine, a red light, red hair, blushing.

phrases.meaning: the common thread, the main line of something

etymology.text: From Middle High German rōt (“red, red-haired”), from Old High German rōt, from Proto-West Germanic *raud, from Proto-Germanic *raudaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rowdʰós, from *h₁rewdʰ-. Compare Dutch rood, English red, Danish rød.

funFacts: The same Indo-European root gave Greek ερυθρός (red – the Ερυθρά Θάλασσα, Red Sea) and Latin ruber.
pitfalls: rot werden = to blush (not “to become red” in general).
subtleties: As a noun a colour is neuter and capitalised: das Rot (ein helles Rot).
Comparison: röter / roter, am rötesten / am rotesten – both exist, rarely needed.
Light and dark shades are one word: hellrot, dunkelrot (ein dunkelrotes Auto).

profile.feeling: Blue – the sky, blue eyes; and, in slang, drunk.

phrases.tr: to promise the blue from the sky

phrases.meaning: a trip with no fixed destination

etymology.text: From Middle High German blā (genitive blāwes), from Old High German blāo, from Proto-West Germanic *blāu, from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz.

funFacts: Russian splits blue into two basic colours, синий (dark) and голубой (light); German, like English, has one: blau, with hellblau and dunkelblau.
pitfalls: blau sein = to be drunk (colloquial) – it never means “sad” like English “feeling blue”.
subtleties: As a noun a colour is neuter and capitalised: das Blau (ein helles Blau).
Comparison exists but is rare for colours: blauer, am blauesten. (am blausten also).
Light and dark shades are one word: hellblau, dunkelblau (ein dunkelblaues Auto).

subtleties: As a noun a colour is neuter and capitalised: das Gelb (ein helles Gelb).
Comparison exists but is rare for colours: gelber, am gelbsten.

profile.feeling: Brown – wood, eyes, a summer tan.

senses.def: Nazi, far-right (politics, from the brown SA uniforms)

examples.text: Nach dem Urlaub bin ich ganz braun.
examples.tr: After the holiday I’m really tanned.

etymology.text: From Middle High German and Old High German brūn, from Proto-West Germanic *brūn.

funFacts: English brown and German braun are one Germanic word.
pitfalls: In political talk braun refers to the Nazis and the far right – mind the context.
subtleties: As a noun a colour is neuter and capitalised: das Braun (ein helles Braun).
Comparison: brauner, am braunsten (colloquial bräuner).

profile.feeling: Grey – a grey sky, grey hair, the grey everyday.

examples.text: Nach dem Urlaub kommt der graue Alltag.
examples.tr: After the holiday comes the dreary daily routine.

phrases.text: sich keine grauen Haare wachsen lassen
phrases.tr: not to let oneself grow grey hairs
phrases.meaning: not to lose sleep over something

synonyms.nuance: greying, flecked with grey – of hair

etymology.text: From Middle High German grā, from Old High German grāo, from Proto-West Germanic *grāu. Compare English gray, grey.

funFacts: eine graue Maus (“a grey mouse”) is a plain, unremarkable person.
pitfalls: English writes grey or gray; German has only grau.
subtleties: As a noun a colour is neuter and capitalised: das Grau (ein helles Grau).
Comparison exists but is rare for colours: grauer, am grauesten. (am grausten also).

profile.feeling: Orange – the colour of the fruit; it takes no endings.

synonyms.nuance: orange-coloured – takes normal endings, the safe choice before a noun

etymology.text: From the noun Orange (“orange fruit”), from French orange.

funFacts: The fruit is also die Apfelsine (“apple from China”) in the north – like Russian апельсин; Greek πορτοκάλι, Turkish portakal and Arabic بُرْتُقَال name it after Portugal.
pitfalls: Before a noun it traditionally stays unchanged: ein orange Kleid, eine orange Tasche, mit dem orange Auto. Everyday speech often adds endings with an extra -n- (ein orangenes Auto) – that is colloquial and many teachers mark it wrong; in writing use it unchanged or the compound orange-farben (ein orangefarbenes Kleid).
subtleties: Pronounced the French way: o-RAHNG-zhe, with the zh of Journal.
Capitalised, die Orange is the fruit.

profile.feeling: Pink – pale pink, the colour of roses; it takes no endings.

examples.text: Er sieht alles durch die rosarote Brille.
examples.tr: He sees everything through rose-tinted glasses.

phrases.text: etwas durch die rosarote Brille sehen
phrases.tr: to see something through the rosy-red glasses
phrases.meaning: to see something through rose-tinted glasses

synonyms.nuance: bright, hot pink – borrowed from English, often declined in speech (ein pinkes T-Shirt)
very pale pink – also the wine

funFacts: rosa is simply Latin rosa, “rose” – Greek ροζ and Russian розовый also name the colour after the rose.
pitfalls: Before a noun it traditionally stays unchanged: ein rosa Kleid, eine rosa Tasche, mit dem rosa Auto. Everyday speech often adds endings with an extra -n- (ein rosanes Kleid) – that is colloquial and many teachers mark it wrong; in writing use it unchanged or the compound rosa-farben (ein rosafarbenes Kleid).
subtleties: rosa is pale pink; strong pink is pink.

profile.feeling: Purple, lilac – the colour of lilac flowers; it takes no endings.

examples.text: Die Kuh in der Werbung ist lila.
examples.tr: The cow in the advert is purple.

synonyms.nuance: violet – a bit more formal and technical

funFacts: The cow in the Milka chocolate adverts has been lila since the 1970s – “die lila Kuh”.
pitfalls: Before a noun it traditionally stays unchanged: ein lila Kleid, eine lila Tasche, mit dem lila Auto. Everyday speech often adds endings with an extra -n- (eine lilane Tasche) – that is colloquial and many teachers mark it wrong; in writing use it unchanged or the compound lila-farben (ein lilafarbenes Kleid).
subtleties: lila covers lilac to purple; very dark purple is dunkellila.
lila is not compared.

profile.feeling: Light, bright – light colours, bright rooms, long summer evenings.

senses.def: bright, light (a room, the day: Es ist hell)

examples.text: Im Sommer ist es lange hell.
examples.tr: In summer it stays light for a long time.

synonyms.nuance: pale – a faint colour; also of faces

etymology.text: From Middle High German hel (“resounding, loud, shining, bright”), from Old High German hel (“resounding”), from Proto-Germanic *halliz (“resounding”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, make noise”). Cognate with Dutch hel.

funFacts: hell first described sound – “ringing, clear” – and only later light; eine helle Stimme is still a clear, high voice.
am helllichten Tag (in broad daylight) has three l’s in a row since the 1996 spelling reform.
pitfalls: hell is not English “hell” (die Hölle), and not “light” in weight (leicht).
subtleties: Shades are one word: hellblau, hellgrün, hellrot.
Comparison: heller, am hellsten.

profile.feeling: Dark – dark colours, dark winter evenings, dark beer.

examples.text: Im Winter wird es früh dunkel.
examples.tr: In winter it gets dark early.

phrases.meaning: to be in the dark, to have no idea

etymology.text: From Middle High German tunkel, from Old High German tunkal, tuncal (“dark”), from Proto-Germanic *dunkalaz (“dark”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʷ- (“to smoke, fume”). Cognate to Dutch donker (“dark”).

funFacts: In Bavaria beer is ordered by its colour: ein Helles or ein Dunkles.
pitfalls: The e before l drops when an ending follows: ein dunkler Anzug, dunkle Haare, das dunkle Bier (not *dunkeles); comparative dunkler.
subtleties: dunkler is both the comparative (darker) and the strong masculine form (ein dunkler Anzug).
Shades are one word: dunkelblau, dunkelrot.

profile.feeling: More – the comparative of viel; with nicht: no longer.

senses.def: more (comparative of viel: mehr Zeit, mehr als …)
no longer, any more (with negation: nicht mehr, kein … mehr)

examples.text: Im Sommer trinken wir mehr Wasser.
examples.tr: In summer we drink more water.

examples.text: Ich habe mehr Bücher als du.
examples.tr: I have more books than you.
He doesn’t live here any more.

phrases.source: attributed to Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 1832

synonyms.nuance: further, additional – an adjective with endings (weitere Fragen)

etymology.text: From Middle High German mēre, from Old High German mēro, from Proto-West Germanic *maiʀō, from Proto-Germanic *maizô, from Proto-Indo-European *mē- (“many”). See English more.

funFacts: mehr and English more are one word, from Proto-Germanic *maizô.
pitfalls: mehr never takes an ending: mehr Bücher, mehr Milch (not *mehre).
nicht mehr = no longer – not “not more”: Ich rauche nicht mehr = I don’t smoke any more.
subtleties: mehrere is a different word: mehrere Bücher = several books.
viel – mehr – am meisten: the comparison of viel.

profile.feeling: The most – the superlative of viel, with a verb: Was magst du am meisten?

senses.def: most, the most (superlative of viel, with a verb)

examples.text: Am meisten freue ich mich auf den Urlaub.
examples.tr: Most of all I’m looking forward to the holiday.

synonyms.nuance: most (+ plural noun): die meisten Leute = most people – a determiner with endings
most of it (das meiste Geld = most of the money)

etymology.text: The superlative of viel (comparative mehr, superlative am meisten). meist- is from Old High German meist, from Proto-Germanic *maist, *maistaz. Compare Dutch meest, English most, Danish mest.

funFacts: meist- and English most are one word.
pitfalls: “Most people / most children” is die meisten Leute / die meisten Kinder, not *am meisten Leute.
subtleties: am meisten is built like am größten, am schnellsten: am + -sten.

profile.feeling: Than – after a comparative; and “when” for one event in the past.

senses.def: when (one event or period in the past: Als ich jung war, …)
as (in the role of: als Lehrer arbeiten)

examples.text: Der Zug ist schneller als der Bus.
examples.tr: The train is faster than the bus.

examples.text: Mein Bruder ist älter als ich.
examples.tr: My brother is older than me.

examples.text: Als ich ein Kind war, wohnten wir in Athen.
examples.tr: When I was a child, we lived in Athens.

examples.text: Als wir ankamen, war es schon dunkel.
examples.tr: When we arrived, it was already dark.

phrases.text: Lieber ein Ende mit Schrecken als ein Schrecken ohne Ende.
phrases.tr: Better an end with horror than horror without end.
phrases.meaning: better to end a bad situation now than suffer it forever

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym for “than”: als is the only word after a comparative in standard German.

etymology.text: From Middle High German alles, from Old High German also, alsō (“as, like”); equivalent to all + so. Compare English as.

funFacts: als comes from all + so – the same pair that gave English also and, worn down, as.
pitfalls: than = als, not wie: größer als ich. *größer wie ich is colloquial/regional and counts as an error in writing; “as … as” is so … wie (so groß wie ich).
After als the pronoun stays nominative: älter als ich (not *als mich).
als (when) is for ONE event or period in the past; for repeated or future events use wenn (S18).
subtleties: A clause with als (when) has the verb at the end: Als ich jung war, …
